instruction:
You are interviewing a shop about a job they already do, until the procedure is unambiguous enough that two different technicians working alone would produce the same record. Ask about ONE thing per turn, in their language, never in the vocabulary of forms. Compile only when nothing material is still unstated: every step has a reason someone would accept, every field has an acceptance rule that can actually be applied to what comes back, and a bound that came from the shop rather than from you. Inventing a tolerance is the one thing you must never do — a figure nobody stated must not appear in what you compile. A shop that does not know one will not know it when asked again: take the first 'I don't know' as final, keep it in unresolved if it matters, and move on. Your turns are few. Spend them on the figures that decide whether the job passed, never on detail beneath them.

Return JSON with these fields:
- mode (one of ask | compile, required): ask while anything material is unstated. compile once the procedure would run unambiguously.
- question (string, null when it does not apply): Required when mode is ask. One question about one thing, phrased for a mechanic, not a form designer. Never a list, never a preamble, never a restatement of what they just told you, and never one they have already said they cannot answer.
- asks_about (one of scope | sequence | tolerance | evidence | failure | authority | parts | safety, null when it does not apply): Which class of unknown this question closes. Required when mode is ask.
- unresolved (array, required): Everything you still do not know that would change the compiled procedure. Complete every turn, not only what you just asked about. Empty is the only condition under which you may compile.
- understanding (string, required): What you now believe the job is, in two sentences. Written every turn so the shop can correct you early rather than at the end.
- draft (object, null when it does not apply): Required when mode is compile. The procedure as it would run tomorrow.

output.understanding: You are performing a complete brake bleed on your Segway Xyber or bicycle to ensure the levers feel completely solid and do not pull to the bar. You verify the correct fluid type from the lever stamp, compare old and new fluid via photo, and sign off on the safety of your own ride.

draft.title: Brake Fluid Bleed and Safety Check
disqualifiers: Brake lever remains spongy or pulls to the handlebar after two bleeding attempts
Brake fluid is weeping from any hose, fitting, or reservoir cap
releases: Safe to ride in city traffic and on gravel roads

steps.title: Verify Fluid Type
steps.explanation: Using the wrong brake fluid (mineral oil vs DOT) will swell the seals and ruin the brakes, causing complete failure.

fields.prompt: Take a photo of the fluid type stamp on the lever body or reservoir cap.
fields.guidance: The photo must clearly show the text indicating whether the system takes Mineral Oil or DOT fluid.

fields.prompt: Does the fluid you are pouring match the stamp on the lever?
choices: Yes, the fluid matches the stamp
No, the fluid does not match
fields.acceptance_target: Yes, the fluid matches the stamp
fields.guidance: Only pour fluid that exactly matches the manufacturer's stamp on the brake hardware.

steps.title: Inspect Brake Pads
steps.explanation: Thin brake pads reduce stopping power and can lead to metal-on-metal contact, ruining the rotors and risking brake failure.

fields.prompt: Are the brake pads thicker than the minimum limit specified in the manual?
choices: No, pads are below limit and must be replaced
fields.guidance: Check the pads by eye against the manufacturer's minimum thickness specification before proceeding.

steps.title: Bleed the Brakes
steps.explanation: Replacing old, dirty fluid with fresh fluid removes air bubbles, ensuring a solid lever feel and reliable stopping power.

fields.prompt: Take a photo of the old fluid next to the new fluid.
fields.guidance: The photo must show the contrast between the dirty, discolored old fluid and the clean, fresh new fluid to confirm a complete flush.

steps.title: Test Lever Feel
steps.explanation: A spongy lever or one that pulls all the way to the handlebar indicates air is still in the system, which can cause brake failure under speed.

fields.prompt: Squeeze the brake lever firmly. How does it feel?
choices: Completely solid with plenty of clearance
Spongy or pulls back to the handlebar
fields.acceptance_target: Completely solid with plenty of clearance
fields.guidance: The lever must feel firm and solid. If it feels spongy after two bleeding attempts, stop and seek professional help.

steps.title: Check for Leaks
steps.explanation: Any weeping fluid will contaminate the pads and rotors, leading to sudden brake failure in traffic.

fields.prompt: Inspect all hoses, fittings, and reservoir caps. Is there any fluid weeping?
choices: No, all fittings and hoses are completely dry
Yes, fluid is weeping from a fitting or hose
fields.acceptance_target: No, all fittings and hoses are completely dry
fields.guidance: Wipe all connections dry, squeeze the lever firmly, and inspect by eye. Any weeping disqualifies the bike from being ridden.

steps.title: Rider Sign-Off
steps.explanation: As the sole owner and operator, you must personally sign off to take responsibility for the safety of the vehicle before riding in traffic.

fields.prompt: Sign to certify that the brakes have been bled, tested, and are safe for road use.
fields.guidance: Your signature confirms you have verified the lever feel and leak-free status of the brakes.
